item.title: What You Gain When You Read for Deep Knowledge
item.description:
Cognition

What You Gain When You Read for Deep Knowledge

Deep reading can make you healthier and wiser.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Deep reading develops powerful thinking.
  • Reading for powerful thinking is more essential today than ever before.
  • Life altering and life sustaining benefits come to those who read deeply.

In 1996, before Google, before Facebook and TikTok, and even before iPhones, Alberto Manguel in his now classic book, A History of Reading, said, “We cannot do but read. Reading, almost as much as breathing, is our essential function.”

To be a reader, Manguel further enlightens us, is to be part of a culture of letters dating from the first Sumerian tablets of the fifth millennium B.C.E. to Greek scrolls, from the codices of St. Augustine to the quartos of Shakespeare, from graphic novels to e-readers and smartwatches. Every word, text, and image read is part of a history of language filled with tales of anarchy, censorship, triumph, and passion. To read, then, is to become part of that history.

As a compulsive reader and idea gatherer, when I got to the epilogue of Leonard Mlodinow’s fascinating book The Upright Thinkers, I found this point to be especially memorable: “Powerful thinking,” he says, “is a craft, and it is one worth doing well.” Now consider that powerful thinking is made possible with language, and reading is a conveyance of language. Let’s reflect on the contributions reading makes to powerful thinking. When we develop this craft, we are able to engage with, integrate, and express complex ideas through reading. In the service of this craft, we purposely select appropriate media to communicate what we know and to share our unique conception about text and the world. And we use text and other related media to enlarge understandings of topics of interest. The more we exercise literate processes, the more we take advantage of—while also increasing—our ability to think powerfully.

Developing and using reading to think powerfully may be more “essential” today than ever before, given the premium placed on flexible expertise in modern work spaces and the importance of critical information literacy in an age of mis/dis-information. Furthermore, an over-reliance on Generative AI, as some experts have cautioned, can drain us of complex and creative thinking. And “Google knowledge” acquired through online searches can produce the appearance of wisdom but often leads to superficial understanding rather than deep comprehension.

The Benefits of Deep Reading—Even Today

Advocating for a culture of deep readers may seem quaint in a world dominated by a ceaseless stream of images and soundbites, indeed a post-typographical world, as some have termed it, but there remain many genuine and life-changing affordances that come to those who practice this literate behavior.

  • For parents who want their children to be high achievers in school, students who are engaged and frequent readers are more successful academically than their peers who show little or no interest in reading. And by extension, those with higher school marks have greater access to additional educational opportunities and, ultimately, to the more lucrative career prospects.
  • Evidence shows that readers are happier and more content than those who cannot or choose not to read. Reading fiction, in particular, has been shown to foster empathy and an appreciation for others. However, reading just about anything in an engaged and immersive way correlates with reduced stress and depression, and higher self-esteem.
  • The medical and public health professions have known for decades that readers lead healthier lives, both physically and mentally. For instance, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has been conducting and supporting systematic study of reading literacy since the 1970s. Difficulty learning to read is viewed by the NIH as a major public health concern as much as an educational challenge. Adults who self-report the worst health also have the most limited literacy, numeracy, and health literacy skills.
  • Perhaps a surprising and unexpected benefit of engaged reading comes from large-scale correlational studies that have demonstrated readers live longer than their non-reading peers. In one study, Yale researchers tracked seniors over the age of 50 for 12 years and discovered book readers had a significantly lower mortality rate compared with non-readers in the same age cohort.

Despite messages to the contrary suggesting reading is a dying art, an obsolete habit, it still holds that those who take advantage of this ever more “essential function” greatly improve the chances for success in their personal, civic, and occupational worlds.

item.title: What Parents Get Wrong About Children's Lies
item.description:
Deception

What Parents Get Wrong About Children's Lies

What developmental research reveals about children's honesty and deception.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Children do not lie solely to avoid punishment or to get what they want.
  • The emergence of lying can be a sign of developing social-cognitive skills.
  • Most children lie occasionally; persistent, frequent lying is far less common.

Discovering that your child lied can be disappointing, frustrating, or even alarming. Many adults interpret lying as a sign that something has gone wrong. Certainly, we do not wish to be lied to and we have to teach children not only the importance of honesty, but also how to be honest. However, we also need to be careful not to overreact. Understanding why children lie can help us respond thoughtfully rather than react out of frustration. Yet some common beliefs about children’s lies are not supported by developmental research. Understanding what lies do (and do not) mean can help parents respond more effectively. Here are five things parents misunderstand about children’s lies.

1. "Good children don't lie."

Almost all children lie at some point. Research with adults show the most adults tell occasional lies (Serota et al, 2010). Does that mean we are all bad people? People lie for many reasons, ranging from self-interest to protecting someone else’s feelings. Lying is a common part of development. As I discussed in my previous blog, lying behaviour emerges alongside children’s developing social-cognitive skills (Lee, 2013). With socialization from those around them, they learn that lying is not an acceptable behaviour, and to lie only occasionally for specific reasons. Honest, well-adjusted children (and adults) sometimes lie. The fact that a child lies does not automatically indicate a character flaw or make them a bad person. The more important question to ask is “why did they lie?” By understanding their motivation, parents can better understand their decision and address the underlying issue.

2. "Lying always means something is wrong."

A lie does not automatically signal a serious problem. Research indicates that occasional lying is common across childhood and adolescence (Talwar et al., 2026). While persistent or serious dishonesty may warrant concern, most children experiment with deception at some point as part of typical social development. As I outlined in my last post, lying, especially in early childhood, can reflect developing cognitive and social abilities. (Talwar & Crossman, 2011) Successful lying requires perspective-taking and self-control. As children develop and strengthen these abilities, their ability to deceive convincingly also improves. The fact that the development of lying is related to their social-cognitive abilities does not make lying desirable, but it does indicate developmental growth. The fact that lying reflects these developing abilities does not make lying desirable, but it does indicate developmental growth. Thus, children’s early lies are often a sign of their burgeoning cognitive abilities. At the same time, these moments create opportunities to teach honesty through conversations, stories, and your own example.

3. "The best way to stop lying is to punish it."

Punishment can stop behaviour in the moment, but it does not always promote honesty in the long run. Our research has found that harsh punishment can sometimes increase dishonesty in the future (Talwar & Lee, 2011). Children who fear severe punishment may become more motivated to hide wrongdoing rather than admit it. Research suggests that emphasizing honesty, open communication, and fair consequences can be more effective than focusing only on punishment. Telling the truth is not always easy, especially when children expect a negative reaction. When children do tell the truth, acknowledging that honesty can encourage more of it in the future. Focusing on the behaviour you want to see, honesty, is often more effective than focusing only on the lie.

4. "All lies are equally concerning."

Not all lies serve the same purpose. Some lies are told to avoid consequences ("No, I didn't break the lamp"). Others are told to gain an advantage ("The teacher said I don't need to do my homework"). Some lies are intended to spare someone's feelings, such as politely thanking a relative for a disappointing gift. Others help maintain relationships, such as reassuring a friend about a small mistake.

These lies are not morally equivalent, and understanding why a child lied is often more important than focusing only on the fact that they lied. The purpose of the lie can help guide a parent's response.

5. "If my child lies, I can never trust them."

We don’t like being lied to in general. When someone close to us lies, it can hurt and feel like a violation of trust. This is often the reason that parents feel so upset when they catch their children lying to them. When we realize someone is not truthful with us, we worry we can’t trust them anymore. However, it is important to remember trust develops through ongoing interactions, not isolated incidents. When you notice your child starting to tell lies, try to view it as a learning opportunity. You can use these moments as an impetus to start having conversations where you discuss honesty, trust, and relationships. These are conversations that evolve over time. With these conversations, children develop stronger moral understanding over time. Thus, a lie is usually a conversation starter, not a final verdict on a child’s character.

We want our children to be honest and teach them the value of honesty. Teaching honesty takes time. Because lies can feel frustrating or hurtful, it is easy to focus only on deception itself. When you catch your child lying, consider what the lie reveals about their thinking, relationships, motivations, and development. By looking beyond the behaviour itself, parents can respond in ways that strengthen honesty and trust.

item.title: Texting Troubles: Illusions and Delusions
item.description:
Relationships

Texting Troubles: Illusions and Delusions

Despite the many benefits of texting, there are also potential pitfalls.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Texting can have unfortunate side effects, such as assumptions that a slower response rate is a rejection.
  • The lack of tone and facial expressions can lead to distortions about messages received.
  • Voice-to-voice or face-to-face conversations are underrated in modern times.

The days of communicating only by mail and waiting weeks or months for a response are long gone. While we may still receive some items by postal service, these are much less frequent and generally much less exciting.

Texting has become the current and often most frequent personal communication of choice.

British software engineer Neil Papworth sent the first text message in 1992, but texting didn’t become widely popular until about 2000. And in 2007, the text message volume officially surpassed phone call volume in the United States.

Email became more popular globally in the mid-1990s and remains a widespread means of communication, but texting surpasses email as the preferred means for quick, day-to-day personal exchanges.

Texting has many advantages, including the ease, simplicity, and accessibility of keeping people more connected. But texting can also create difficulties, especially around relationship assumptions.

In my work as a therapist (and as a person living in this modern world), I have noticed and like to name two domains where trouble with texting seems to most often arise: illusions of immediacy and delusional-like distortions.

Illusions of Immediacy

We know that most people have their phones on them or with them often around the clock; however, this does not mean everyone is immediately available or instantly able to respond.

Source: That Guy Craig/Pexels

Every person naturally has different schedules, routines, and processing styles. While some comments or questions in the context of an upcoming meeting might be expected to be addressed promptly (such as “Where are we meeting for lunch?”), the more complex statements or queries often need more time or consideration (such as “I am concerned about what you said last night”).

Although most people check texts more often and more quickly than emails, the assumption that someone has read another’s text and can respond immediately is not reasonable in all contexts. Someone may also have seen a message but not been ready to respond for a multitude of reasons.

This illusion of immediacy can be a significant source of angst and aggravation. We humans often jump to conclusions if we don’t get a response as immediately as expected, and we can sometimes create stories in our minds about why there might be a delay (such as “She hasn’t responded; she must be angry with me” or “He probably doesn’t care that I am hurt”).

A lack of something or the delay of response is not the full story. Receivers often interpret a missing or delayed response from the sender with much greater meaning than is typically warranted, especially if the receiver is feeling more on edge or has set some internalized expectations. And because humans have a negativity bias, pessimistic suppositions are often made.

Part of why this happens in texting can be because there might often be a rapid back-and-forth that happens between two individuals, but then there is a shift in the response rate. Having had most of the exchanges be more instantaneous one hour does not mean that immediacy is always available or even appropriate in the following hour. This can be confusing or jarring, but this needs more consideration of the context (“They might be having a busy day”) rather than assuming a character flaw (“They are so self-centered”).

Pausing until we have the particulars, slowing down the stories, and finding out the facts are all highly recommended.

Delusional-like Distortions

The other interpersonal difficulty that arises can occur when someone receives a somewhat brief, cryptic, or unexpected text response and makes assumptions about the sender’s intention.

Source: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash

Guesses and conjectures are made, sometimes of significant magnitude, and they can be delusion-like distortions or major misconceptions. A simple text response of “OK” might be interpreted as “They are mad” or “She doesn’t really want to do that.” The receiver, expecting questions or sympathy in response to sharing important information, might instead interpret a simple encouraging sentiment as “They don’t want to talk about this” or “He doesn’t understand what a big deal this is to me.”

By adding an interpretation based on our assumptions, we are inserting something into the situation without having all the data. Jumping to a conclusion without complete knowledge or understanding of the sender’s intent can lead to negative spirals, especially if the receiver is feeling more vulnerable or sensitive about the information being referenced.

This is more likely to happen in texting because a large portion of communication is nonverbal. Words matter, but tone, facial expression, and body language matter too. And because texting does not allow for the latter factors, we are left to fill in the blanks with our own potentially flawed analysis. Assumptions are, by nature, subjective and biased by our own perspective, and we are not mind-readers.

Again, it's important to step back for a broader perspective, consider alternative explanations, and seek a more dedicated conversation with the source.

Texts Can Be Tricky

The cognitive biases that occur in sensitive texting topics can hurt our relationships.

Source: Samuel Angor/Unsplash

Texting troubles often involve a heuristic trap of using a mental shortcut that might not fit the situation. This can involve letting our subjective thinking guide the conclusions, such as “I would have responded more quickly” or “If I said this sort of thing, it would mean I don’t care.” This is a negatively biased interpretation with selective attention to the negative.

This human tendency towards confirmation bias (seeking out and noticing only data that supports our worldview), especially under distress, is not conscious – but it does require conscious intervention to change. Rather than rigidly gripping only the pieces of information that seem to confirm our beliefs, we can practice the pattern of expanding our lens to also look for alternative explanations and examples of positive connection.

No Substitute for Direct, Real-Time Conversations

Some topics are simply better handled in person or at least with a live conversation.

Source: Priscilla Du Preez/Unsplash

Texting is a great way to have quick, efficient exchanges or to explore deeper-level topics that aren’t time-sensitive, overly emotional, or overly nuanced; however, a face-to-face or voice-to-voice conversation can often enrich and clarify so much.

Sometimes a real conflict or misunderstanding has occurred, and in certain circumstances it may need relational repair; other times, it needs clarification rather than repair. Asking honest questions and mindfully listening to responses in a curiously compassionate way are key.

Texts might seem like a comprehensive summary of a situation, but there is so much more to relationships. Just as the script for a play requires actors to do more than just say the words and leads directors to help contextualize the interactions on stage, humans too need to look beyond the words and aim to open up to understanding from multiple angles. And this is much better done directly.

item.title: Childfree Midlife Millennials
item.description:
Midlife

Childfree Midlife Millennials

Personal Perspective: Does the midlife crisis hit different when you don’t have kids?

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Midlife crises of childfree millennials look different than those of people who took a more traditional path.
  • Childfree millennials have fewer obligations to contend with as they contemplate their second acts.
  • Midlife is the last biological off-ramp from a childfree path, the last opportunity to change your mind.

Leading up to my 40th birthday, I didn’t anticipate a midlife crisis. I was fresh off the heels of one existential roundabout, the "to be or not to be" parenthood dilemma. Didn’t I get a pass? An exemption? Credit for time served? Hadn’t I individuated and self-actualized enough? Apparently not.

One crisis doesn't preclude you from another

My midlife crisis came about nine months after the big 4-0, as if it had to gestate like a baby. Seemingly out of nowhere, I was grappling with the realities of aging (my back hurts when I sneeze and I have high cholesterol?!). Not to mention the pesky problem of my mortality—life was likely half over (at best!). Just because I didn’t have a kid didn’t mean I was exempt from tangoing with these realities.

In pop culture and media, the midlife narrative usually focuses on parents. Their kids no longer need, want, or like having them around. They no longer recognize their romantic partner turned co-parent. They have newfound time and energy to feel and process emotions after years on autopilot. And the prognosis is usually not positive. They are stuck in a career rut in an unfulfilling corporate role, disenfranchised with the suburban life and nuclear family they were told would provide meaning. That’s the midlife crisis we know by heart.

Millennials are the first generation to opt out of parenthood in large numbers, thanks to factors good and bad (good: increased awareness and agency; bad: cost of living and the likelihood of climate catastrophe). Without children and the traditional life path, what shape does our midlife malaise take?

How the childfree midlife crisis is similar... And different

In many ways, it can be similar. We grapple with deteriorating health and aging (ours and that of our loved ones). We have careers that pale in comparison to what we thought we’d accomplish. We are driven to do an inventory of our lives and decide how to enhance the ROI of what’s left. That brings me to a major benefit of the childfree midlife crisis. We have fewer obligations and more flexibility to make big moves, write our own scripts, and take risks to jump-start our second act.

But it ain’t all sunshine. Many childfree middle-aged women return to the question they had put to bed, only to find it reawakening like a teething baby. Am I sure I don’t want kids?

Middle age is the last biological off-ramp from the childfree path. Your reproductive window only remains open a crack, and it’s now or never if you want to change your mind a final time—as everyone has been telling you you’d do since you revealed your childfree choice.

Aubrey Plaza, a celebrity who had a child at midlife
Source: Bryan Berlin, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

At midlife, we see female celebrities make the leap into motherhood after years of deferring and demurring. Hilary Swank just announced she’s pregnant with her third child—at 52. My grandmother was younger than that when I was born. Of course, celebrities have a lot more options than we mere mortals (access to the latest medical interventions, surrogates, and full-time nannies once the babies are born). But as humans, it’s hard not to compare yourself to those held up to us as the ideal. Aubrey Plaza, Cameron Diaz, and Eva Mendes are all recent examples of famous women we thought—or at least hoped—were childfree who had a child (or children) later in life.

And it’s not that we aren’t happy for them to follow the path that’s best for them, but it can feel like we’ve lost them to the other side.

You'll change your mind

It also reinforces the "You’ll change your mind" narrative that has always sounded vaguely threatening to me. When people say you’ll change your mind to brush off your carefully considered decision, it can feel like you’re childish, immature, and just haven’t seen the light yet. It also doesn’t take into account that you may have already changed your mind. I certainly did—a dozen or more times. I flip-flopped and fence-sat through my 20s and 30s and even wrote a book about it.

I always assumed that I would have kids one day, and it was only through disentangling myself from societal and cultural messaging and unlearning a lot of beliefs that I was able to say with confidence and conviction that I do not want to have children. Changing your mind can be a gift if it’s measured and considered and not a panic-fueled split-second decision. Staying true to your carefully considered and hard-won path can also be a gift.

My doctor laughed when I recently expressed disappointment that my blood work showed I am not yet in perimenopause or menopause. I know that change will bring about its own challenges, but I’m so excited for that reproductive window to finally close. The latch will be secured, a padlock attached, and maybe some boards will be nailed over the frame for good measure. Then—at last—I can smile smugly at the folks who told me I’d change my mind.

Conclusions

Like everything else, the midlife crisis hits a little different when you don’t have kids, but it still exists. Who knows how many healthy years you have left. If there are any big moves or bold steps you want to take, this is the moment. And you can do so without jeopardizing the well-being of your (nonexistent) kids.

The childfree midlife crisis need not involve a Hail Mary pregnancy and last-minute biological legacy. Maybe you’ll move to the country or to another country. Maybe you’ll quit your job to pursue your dream full-time. Maybe you’ll start a revolution or a religion. It’s your one wild and precious childfree millennial midlife crisis. Use it wisely.

item.title: Good Communication Begins Before We Open Our Mouths
item.description:
Forgiveness

Good Communication Begins Before We Open Our Mouths

The often-overlooked importance of listening to ourselves before speaking.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Good communication starts by noticing what we're feeling before we speak.
  • Defensive reactions can hide more vulnerable feelings, such as hurt, loneliness, or fear.
  • Pausing and sensing into the body can help us speak from our feelings rather than blame.
  • Listening to how our words land helps build trust, understanding, and connection.
Source: Pexels image by Antoni Shkraba

Much has been written about the importance of good communication. But one essential ingredient is often overlooked.

To communicate effectively, we need to know what we’re actually experiencing inside us. Often our first impulse is governed by the fight, flight, freeze, or fawn response wired into us to protect us from real or imagined threats to our physical or emotional safety. We don't have to be hijacked by our nervous system’s protective instincts; instead, we can pause long enough to uncover what we’re actually experiencing inside.

Vulnerability can feel threatening to the protective parts of us that are organized around emotional and physical survival. We can tap into another part of ourselves to access the more vulnerable feelings underlying our initial reaction. We can slow down enough to help settle our nervous system and bring gentle, curious attention to what we're experiencing inside.

As I explore in my book, The Power of Gentle Presence, learning to meet our inner experience with gentleness and curiosity can help us become less defensive and more available for meaningful connection.

Communication Based on Our Felt Experience

Communication often becomes more effective when we move beyond our first reactions and express the more vulnerable feelings underneath them. We might think we're expressing our true feelings when we are actually venting a defensive reaction. For example, we might attack while congratulating ourselves for being “honest.” “I really feel that you’re self-centered.” “I feel that you only think about yourself.”

Of course, these aren’t descriptions of our real feelings—they’re judgments and criticisms disguised as feelings. What are we actually feeling when someone offends us, neglects us, or doesn’t meet us where we want to be met? Someone can sincerely believe their partner is selfish and express that judgment forcefully. But they may not realize that beneath their anger lie more vulnerable feelings of loneliness, hurt, or fear of disconnection.

By accessing these primary feelings, we might say: "I've been feeling lonely lately, and I'm missing the closeness we used to have."

It takes courageous self-awareness to pause long enough to access feelings that may be threatening or overwhelming. In Internal Family Systems language, these feelings may come from a hurt part of ourselves that we pushed away—parts we've tried to keep out of awareness because their feelings are scary or uncomfortable.

No matter how many communication skills trainings we have completed or communication books we have read, our communication may fall short if we can't access these deeper layers of our felt experience.

Three Steps Toward Better Communication

If you want to communicate more effectively:

Slow down: Before speaking, slow down, take a breath, and put attention on the body. What sensations are we noticing? Is our stomach jumpy, our throat constricted, our chest tight?

Simply noticing what we’re experiencing without trying to change it lets uncomfortable feelings settle. Then, instead of acting out our feelings by attacking or shutting down, we have more bandwidth to notice them and speak from them.

Speak from your real feelings: Sometimes what feels like honesty is actually our initial defensive reaction. Pausing allows us to discover what's beneath it and show what's really happening in our heart.

Communication skills training often emphasizes using "I" statements—sharing what we're feeling rather than criticisms or judgments. That may sound simple enough, but it's not easy to confront feelings that may be scary or uncomfortable. It takes self-awareness and courage—a willingness to welcome both pleasant and unpleasant emotions.

Be open to listening: Communication means being willing to hear how our words are landing with the other person. After expressing our feelings, needs, and concerns, keeping our hearts and ears open to how we're affecting others goes a long way toward building trust and connection—which, after all, is probably what we're most wanting.

We can be absolutely sincere in our communication and still not be communicating our deeper truth. Good communication begins not with finding the perfect words, but with a willingness to pause, turn inward, and discover what we're actually feeling. When we speak from that deeper awareness—and remain open to hearing the other person—we create a safer path toward mutual understanding and connection.
